personality_voice.book_baseline: Ernie Macmillan in the books is defined by a highly recognizable personality cluster: pomposity and self-importance (he puffs out his chest, speaks in loud carrying voices, drops his voice 'mysteriously,' and brags about his nine generations of pure-blood ancestry and his revision hours); moral courage mixed with social anxiety (he confronts Harry directly but trembles while doing so, and hesitates before signing the DA list out of prefect-duty concern); an eagerness to be seen as important and authoritative (he speaks 'portentously,' says things like 'Well said!' and 'I personally believe you one hundred per cent'); a tendency toward self-correction and apology when wrong (his formal apology to Harry in CoS); and competitive vanity (he rashly invents his own potion to outshine Harry, resulting in a purple dumpling). His speech is distinctively verbose, formal, and declarative. He uses phrases like 'I mean to say,' 'I personally,' 'I might tell you,' and 'in case you're getting ideas.' He is simultaneously pompous and genuinely well-meaning.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Ernie serves several distinct narrative functions across multiple volumes: (1) In CoS, he is a primary driver of the 'Harry as suspect' subplot — he orchestrates suspicion among Hufflepuffs, confronts Harry directly, and later publicly recants, which marks a turning point in Harry's social rehabilitation. (2) In GoF, he provides social texture as a Hufflepuff loyalist supporting Cedric. (3) In OotP, he is one of the first to publicly and loudly declare belief in Harry at the Hog's Head, is a key DA member, performs in DA sessions, voices the prefect anxiety about the DA list, confronts Malfoy over point-docking, reports Umbridge's failed attempt on Dumbledore's office, and participates in the train ambush against Malfoy. (4) In HBP, he is Harry's Potions table partner, asks the key question about Felix Felicis, provides comic contrast in brewing scenes, sycophantically engages Slughorn, and greets Harry at the Dark Mark scene. (5) In DH, he stands up in the Great Hall to demand the right to fight, is present in the Room of Requirement, and casts a Patronus to save Harry, Ron, and Hermione from dementors. His agency is consistently active: he initiates confrontations, makes public declarations, volunteers information, takes sides, casts spells that change outcomes.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Ernie's motivations in the books are consistently readable: (1) a desire to be seen as important, authoritative, and right — drives his public accusations, his loud declarations of support, his revision-boasting, his sycophancy toward Slughorn; (2) genuine moral concern and a sense of duty — drives his prefect hesitation about the DA list, his apology to Harry, his standing up in the Great Hall; (3) social and status anxiety — drives his pure-blood pride speech (defensive self-protection), his nervousness when Harry confronts him, his trembling; (4) loyalty to Hufflepuff and Cedric — drives his GoF behavior. The internal conflict between wanting to be important/correct and the possibility of being wrong is the engine of his CoS arc: he accuses Harry confidently, trembles when Harry confronts him, but stubbornly maintains his position, and only recants publicly when the evidence is overwhelming. This contradiction — pompous certainty colliding with moral correction — is his most interesting internal feature.

character_arc.book_baseline: Ernie's most complete arc spans CoS: he begins as the confident, pompous ringleader of anti-Harry sentiment among Hufflepuffs, escalates through a direct confrontation with Harry (trembling but stubborn), maintains his position even as doubt creeps in, and ultimately makes a formal, public apology when the evidence exonerates Harry — an act that costs him something in terms of pride. This arc is a miniature study in how moral courage and pomposity coexist: it takes more courage for a proud person to admit they were wrong. Across later books his arc is essentially flat (he is a reliable, loyal, somewhat pompous ally), which is appropriate for a secondary character. The DH Patronus moment represents a culmination of his DA loyalty arc.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Ernie's complexity in the books lies in the productive contradiction between his pomposity and his genuine moral courage. He is not simply comic relief or simply a loyal ally — he is both simultaneously. His CoS scenes show him as simultaneously frightened (trembling, white lips) and stubborn, genuinely wrong but genuinely principled, capable of cruelty (the accusations) and genuine grace (the formal apology). His OotP scenes show him as simultaneously self-important (the revision hours monologue, the prefect badge, the loud 'Well said!') and genuinely committed (signing the DA list despite anxiety, casting a Patronus in battle). His HBP scenes add competitive vanity (the purple dumpling incident), sycophancy (toward Slughorn), and social texture. The pure-blood pride speech — defensive and anxious — adds a dimension that complicates any simple reading of him as a good-natured Hufflepuff. He is also one of the few secondary characters who changes his mind publicly and formally, which requires a specific kind of moral character.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films reduce Ernie to: one moment of public bravery (DH2 Great Hall), background presence in DA scenes, and background presence in the Room of Requirement.
